stimulus.source_note: Photograph: American Indian Movement member at the Wounded Knee occupation, 1973 (Alliance Times-Herald photograph, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons); the photograph was viewed before writing. Account drawn from the grounding books and verified against HISTORY timelines: occupation began February 27, 1973 and ended May 8, 1973, lasting 71 days; Wounded Knee was the site of the 1890 killing of Lakota people.
stimulus.text:
The photograph shows the back of an American Indian Movement member at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in 1973. His jacket reads "AIM" and "INDIAN & PROUD," and he holds a rifle.

On February 27, 1973, about 200 Oglala Lakota and American Indian Movement members took over the town of Wounded Knee, on the Pine Ridge Reservation. They chose the town because federal troops had killed Lakota people there in 1890, and they demanded that the government honor its treaties. Federal agents surrounded the town, and the occupation lasted 71 days, until May 8, 1973.

stem: Why did the occupiers choose Wounded Knee as the site of their protest?

options.text: It was the headquarters of the Bureau of Indian Affairs
options.misconception: Background: The Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters is in Washington, D.C., not Wounded Knee.

options.text: It was the largest city on the Pine Ridge Reservation
options.misconception: The passage does not call Wounded Knee the largest city on the reservation; it calls it the site of the 1890 killings.

options.text: It was the place where the American Indian Movement had been founded
options.misconception: Background: The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968, not at Wounded Knee.

options.text: It was where federal troops killed Lakota people in 1890

rationales.A: Background: The Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters is in Washington, D.C., not at Wounded Knee.
rationales.B: The passage gives the reason for the choice as the 1890 killings, not the town's size.
rationales.C: Background: The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968, not at Wounded Knee.
rationales.D: The passage says the occupiers chose Wounded Knee because federal troops had killed Lakota people there in 1890, and they demanded that the government honor its treaties.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says the occupiers chose Wounded Knee because federal troops had killed Lakota people there in 1890.
2. That history made the town a symbol of broken promises, not just a place on a map.
3. Their demand matched the symbol: they asked the government to honor its treaties.
4. Background: The occupiers also protested the tribal government on Pine Ridge, but the site itself was chosen for the 1890 killings.
Remember: Protesters pick places that already carry meaning, so the place itself helps make their argument.
